newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac backs Spain on EMU at summit.
newsitem.headline: Chirac backs Spain on EMU at summit.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac praised Spain on Monday for its "very courageous" efforts to prepare for European monetary union in 1999, presidential spokeswoman Catherine Colonna said.
Chirac delivered his message of support in talks with Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar at a Franco-Spanish summit amid high security in this Mediterranean port town.
"The President hailed the excellent efforts made by Spain," Colonna told reporters during the talks which began on Monday evening. He described them as "very courageous", she added.
Aznar, whose government unveiled a tough deficit-cutting budget in September, repeated that Spain aimed to join the European Union's single currency in 1999, she said.

Chirac, who sparked a diplomatic row with Rome last month by questioning Italy's chances of joining a single EU currency from the start in 1999, appeared to have switched to a message of hope that both Spain and Italy would be ready in time.
"We hope that they will be there in 1999 while respecting the (Maastricht treaty) criteria," Colonna told a news conference ahead of the summit.
Chirac and Aznar met amid heightened security following a bomb attack early on Monday on the main post office in the town of Aix-en-Provence, 30 km away.
Corsican separatists claimed responsibility for the bombing which badly damaged the building but caused no injuries.

The summit, which also included finance, defence and foreign affairs ministers, was due to run until late on Monday and continue on Tuesday morning, with a closing news conference planned for 1030 GMT on Tuesday.

Spain and Italy have long been regarded as lagging behind frontrunners like Germany in getting their finances and public deficits to fulfil the strict criteria of the Maastricht treaty on economic and monetary union.

But they have followed hard on the heels of France with budget plans in recent months aimed at cutting public deficits next year -- the crucial year for qualification -- to three percent of gross domestic product (GDP), one of the key Maastricht prerequisites for joining monetary union in 1999.

Although the summit was ostensibly devoted to plans for a single "euro" currency, the two countries also used the meeting to air ideas for intervention to relieve the plight of more than a million refugees fleeing fighting in Zaire.
Chirac and Aznar agreed to "unite their efforts" and prepare a "temporary effort to ensure security" in eastern Zaire.

They issued a statement saying: "The two countries will take part in an international meeting to prepare this operation to which they are prepared to contribute and which should be decided by the U.N. Security Council".

French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette, said: "What we're proposing is that the international community -- Europe, the United States, African states -- organise so that there is a security force on the ground to guarantee people's safety."
"France is willing to take part on the strict condition that there is an American, European and African participation," he said in a television interview in Marseille.
Asked whether France would send troops to Zaire, Chirac's spokeswoman Colonna said: "It is a possibility which we are considering".
